cards.q: Am I solving the right problem?
cards.plain: Ask 'why?' to climb to the bigger goal and 'how?' to climb down to a practical step, so you solve the right problem.
cards.answer: We work on the rung "more sales for each dong". The rung above, profit, needs margin data we do not have.
cards.lights: circle 3 · benefits, up the ladder to profit

cards.q: Do I need an innovative solution to a complex problem?
cards.plain: Break a problem into the basic facts you are sure of, then build up from those.
cards.answer: ROAS covers sales and spend only. It cannot prove profit until we know margin and returns.
cards.lights: insight E · what we can prove

cards.plain: What you see happen is the tip. Look for the patterns and causes underneath, and fix those.
cards.answer: Fixing single ad sets treats the event. The structures below keep making it happen, so the moves target them.
cards.lights: insight C · we have the tool, not the fix

cards.plain: Draw the parts of a system and the arrows between them, to spot loops that feed themselves.
cards.answer: Loop 1 and Loop 2 feed a weak signal. Loop 3 means more budget lowers sales per dong. That is why money moves in steps.

cards.q: Am I only thinking of ideal solutions?
cards.plain: Ask what would make the plan fail, then plan to avoid that.
cards.answer: Each bad plan has a guard. The guards shape the plan in step 6.

cards.q: Can I break this problem down?
cards.plain: Split one big question into smaller questions, like branches on a tree.
cards.answer: The 11 moves sit under 6 of the 7 branches on the Questions page.
cards.lights: circle 2 · problems as an issue tree

cards.q: How do I come up with a creative solution?
cards.plain: A six-step routine for solving a problem, from 'what is going on?' to 'align resources'.
cards.answer: 11 moves answer the 6 branch questions. 6 of the 10 most common pieces of advice are among them.

cards.q: What kind of decision am I making?
cards.plain: Sort a decision as a no-brainer, a hard choice or a big choice, so you know how much care it needs.
cards.answer: 5 of the 11 moves are no-brainers: decide fast. 5 are hard choices and 1 is a big choice: Move US chat budget (G4), so all 6 get a small test first. The impact line is 10% of an account's spend assumed.

cards.q: How should I respond to this situation?
cards.plain: Sort a situation as clear, complicated, complex or chaotic, because each needs a different way to act.
cards.answer: Nothing here is chaotic. 3 moves are clear, 4 are complicated (they need analysis) and 4 are complex, so those 4 get small tests first.

cards.q: Which option from these is the best one?
cards.plain: Score each option on the things that matter, then add up the scores to compare them.
cards.answer: G4 scores highest. G7 scores low because it moves no budget. It still runs this month: it is quick and makes ROAS fairer to read.

cards.plain: Check each step from the facts you picked to the belief you hold, so you do not jump to conclusions.
cards.answer: Climbing down changed the plan: we move half, not all, and each step has a test.

cards.q: What would be the long-term consequences of this decision?
cards.plain: Ask what happens after the first effect, and what happens after that.
cards.answer: Each first effect hides a second one. Review v3 traced them for 4 of the 11 moves, and each traced one has a test that would catch it. For the other 7 moves, this demo proposes a later effect and a check to run first, marked as proposed.
cards.lights: circle 4 · how each move is measured

cards.q: What should I be working on right now?
cards.plain: Sort tasks by urgent and important, to decide what to do now, schedule, hand off or leave for later.
cards.answer: Do now: Move VN engagement budget (G1), Merge 7 chat ad sets (G3), Move US chat budget (G4). Also now: Let Meta choose US placements (G5), Exclude past buyers (G7). These match this month's pick. Urgency decides this list, not how hard each move is.

iceberg.text: VN engagement ad sets returned ROAS 0.25 on 152.4M VND. The US chat-purchase goal returned 0.97 (all measured).
Money sits on cheap results. 59.1% (measured) of VN spend chases chats and 26.5% (measured) chases engagement. The US goal gets about 1 (assumed) result a week.

No ad set excludes past buyers with a customer audience; other exclusion settings and actual reach were not checked. 24 of 26 (inferred from ad set names) VN chat ad sets share one audience. Chat sales sit outside the website pixel. No order data is joined.
Our guess, to confirm with the team: more chats mean more sales, cheap results mean efficient ads, and Meta's ROAS equals profit.

group.rule: Each tool sits in exactly one of 7 groups, as set in the feature map. The map was built from Meta for Business pages and the Meta developer docs, read 22 November 2026. Groups are ordered by their best-ranked tool: the group that holds the top-ranked tool comes first. A tie goes to the group with the higher total score. Group size does not decide.
group.excludes: Inside a group, ranked tools come first by rank; tools with fewer than 2 public sources are not ranked and keep Meta's page order.

branch.rule: The issue-tree question the tool mainly helps answer. If it helps two, it goes to the one earlier in the money chain: tracking, audience, creative, bidding, after the click, profit.
branch.excludes: 'Running the account' holds only access, policy and admin tools, which never move sales directly.

benefit.rule: The profit lever the tool is built to move: more sales, cheaper sales, true numbers, a safe account or less work.
benefit.excludes: A tool judged by a cost metric but built to win results (the campaign goals, lookalikes, formats) keeps 'more sales'. 'Cheaper sales' is listed as its second lever.

stage.rule: The funnel stage of the tool's main metric: delivery, attention, conversion, value, profit; or signal and account health. A metric that names two stages takes the later one.
stage.excludes: The earlier stage is kept as the tool's second stage. Reporting, API and account-health tools take 'signal and account health' even when their metric names a funnel stage; each is listed with a reason.

summary: Keep your 4 circles as the picture people see.
Read the logic as a chain: tool → change → benefit → goal (a Benefits Dependency Network). Each benefit has a place for an owner and a measure; no owner is assigned yet.
Turn each benefit into a question and one number to watch (Goal-Question-Metric).
framework.why: Keep the circles as the audience picture, but run the logic as a Benefits Dependency Network. It links platform features through prerequisite and ongoing changes to benefits, each with a measure and a place for an owner. It also supports both demo entry points. Use GQM to turn each benefit into a question and metric.

mapping.circle1: Features now = BDN 'IT enablers' (the means): the platform capabilities available today.
mapping.circle2: Problems = BDN business drivers and 'existing problems or constraints to remove'. In the problem-based build they set the improvement targets and investment objectives.
mapping.circle3: Business benefits = BDN 'benefits' (each with an owner and a measure) rolling up to 'investment objectives'. Each benefit is also a GQM goal.
mapping.circle4: Split it in two. 'How features are used' = BDN 'business changes' (permanent new ways of working). 'How measured' = GQM questions and metrics attached to each benefit.
mapping.insights: Treat each overlap as a directed BDN arrow: a testable claim, not shared membership. 1∩2: an enabler removes a constraint. 2∩3: removing the problem yields a benefit or objective. 3∩4: benefit → GQM question → metric. 4∩1: feature → the business change that uses it.
mapping.actions: Centre chain = BDN 'enabling changes' (one-off prerequisites, e.g. tracking set-up, catalog, audience build, test set-up). They feed 'business changes' (ongoing practices), each with an owner. Order follows the arrows. Starting from business questions builds right-to-left. Starting from the features checklist builds left-to-right and needs a pilot or lift test before scaling. That gives the test-backed plan.

misses: Direction: Venn overlaps show shared membership, but the logic is a cause-and-effect chain (feature → change → benefit → objective).
In a ring of four circles, non-neighbour pairs (features–benefits, problems–metrics) have no overlap, yet feature → benefit is the key claim.
No split between one-off prerequisites (enabling changes) and ongoing practices (business changes), which is what makes the action chain readable.
No owner for each benefit and each action.
No explicit business objective above the benefits (the 'why' the benefits roll up to).
Circle 4 merges usage and measurement, and there is no rule that every benefit gets a question, metric, baseline and test.
No rule for the two entry points: the build should run right-to-left from business questions, and left-to-right from features with a pilot.
caveats: None of these frameworks has been validated for reviewing ad platforms. Their evidence comes from IS, software engineering, programme evaluation and consumer research.
BDN is published in MIS Quarterly Executive. We did not check what kind of evidence its article holds.

Every arrow, in BDN, a strategy map or the circles, is a hypothesis. Nørreklit (2000) shows that scorecard causal links are often assumed rather than shown, so each arrow needs a test (for example a lift test).
Avoid DIKW as structure (critiqued as unsound by Frické 2009). JTBD is useful wording for circle 2 but is a practitioner source.
